newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tens of thousands mark Tiananmen in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Tens of thousands mark Tiananmen in Hong Kong.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Hong Kong people flocked to a local park on Wednesday to honour the victims of Beijing's bloody 1989 crackdown in Tiananmen Square, just 27 days before the British colony reverts to communist-ruled China.

While authorities over the border in China staged a tight security clampdown to avert any anniversary protests, more than 55,000 Hong Kong people thronged to the candlelit mourning vigil on the eighth anniversary of the June 4 Tiananmen massacre.

The sheer weight of the crowd forced organisers to delay the official start of the annual vigil by half an hour. Organisers had placed newspaper advertisements urging people to remember the anniversary amid fears that China would declare future protests taboo.

Many Hong Kong people fear their annual peaceful yet poignant tribute to the victims of the military crackdown will be outlawed after Britain hands its wealthy colony of 6.4 million people over to China at midnight on June 30.

Sitting peacefully in the crowd were grandmothers, students and young parents with children not born when the tanks rolled into Tiananmen Square and crushed the student-led pro-democracy movement with a heavy loss of life.
All cupped flickering candles. Some wept as they sang rousing pro-democracy anthems. Others pumped their arms defiantly in the air and vowed to return year after year, no matter what.
"Eight years -- 2,922 days and nights -- have passed. Tonight we are again using sparks of candlelight, solidified drops of tears to remember you and to mourn you," read one tribute.
Mourning wreaths were propped around the park and billboards and banners read "Never forget June 4".

Huge video screens in the park beamed speeches by pro-democracy activists, many of them denounced as subversive by Beijing. The images competed with the glare of neon signs in the surrounding tourist district.
"I think some people think it's the last time that it will be allowed but most people will come, they will just come next year," said Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's Democracy Party.

More than one million Hong Kong people took to the streets in June 1989 to express shock and revulsion over the brutality of their future leaders which sparked a middle-class exodus from Hong Kong and gave birth to the territory's democracy movement. Simon So, who said he had missed only one rally in the past eight years, brought his five-year-old daughter along for the first time.
"The next generation must be taught never to forget," So, a computer engineer, said.
Activists denounced Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa, Beijing's appointee to run Hong Kong when Britain withdraws, for calling on the population to abandon Tiananmen protests.

Several times over the past week Tung has called in interviews for people to leave behind the "June 4 baggage" and look to the future. "Mr Tung should have come here tonight to see how peaceful the people are," Lee told reporters.
Lee has angered Tung by campaigning overseas against Tung's plans to dilute civil liberties, including curbs on demonstrations in the name of social stability.
"Mr Tung should go to see the Beijing leaders and ask them to reverse the verdict of June 4," Lee said. "It was not a counter-revolutionary or criminal movement. It was a patriotic movement."
